Algebra I · Lesson 8.4

Graphing Inequalities

Solve this lesson →All lessons

A solved inequality is a boundary together with a direction, and drawing it means being exact about both, which side of the boundary the solutions lie on and whether the boundary itself is one of them. On a number line those are a direction and a single circle, and in the plane they are a side of a line together with how that line is drawn.

Problem
The solutions of 4x+7≥834x+7≥83 fill a ray on the number line, running right from a single point. Enter the number where the ray starts.
Show a hint
  • The point at the end of the ray is the value where the two sides come out exactly equal, so start by solving.
  • Subtracting 77 from both sides leaves 4x≥764x≥76, and 44 is positive, so dividing by it leaves the direction alone.
Show the full solution
Subtract 77 from both sides for 4x≥764x≥76, then divide by the positive 44 for x≥19x≥19​. At x=19x=19 the left side is exactly 8383, and 83≥8383≥83 is true, so the ray starts at 1919 and includes that point.
Problem
On a number line the endpoint of a solution ray is drawn as an open circle when that endpoint is not a solution and as a filled circle when it is. Solve 6x+13>556x+13>55, put the boundary number you get back into the inequality, and enter the word, open or filled, for the circle at that endpoint.
Show a hint
  • The circle at the endpoint answers one yes or no question, whether the boundary number itself satisfies 6x+13>556x+13>55.
  • Isolating xx gives x>7x>7, so the endpoint is 77. Put 77 into the left side and compare what you get against 5555 under a strict >>.
Show the full solution
Subtracting 1313 gives 6x>426x>42, and dividing by 66 gives x>7x>7. Putting 77 back in gives 55>5555>55, which is false, so 77 is not a solution and its circle is openopen​. Everything to the right of 77 is shaded and 77 itself is not. With ≥≥ in place of >>, that one point would be a solution and the circle would be filled.
Key idea
On a number line the graph of an inequality is a ray, with a circle at its end. The graph is every point whose coordinate makes the statement true, so the graph of x>7x>7 is everything to the right of 77 and the graph of x<7x<7 is everything to the left. An open circle means the boundary value is excluded and a filled circle means it is included. The graphs of x>7x>7 and x≥7x≥7 are the same ray apart from that one point, so the circle is the only difference between the two pictures.
Problem
The chain −5<2x+3≤17−5<2x+3≤17 says both −5<2x+3−5<2x+3 and 2x+3≤172x+3≤17 at once, so its solutions graph as a single segment of the number line. Enter how many integers satisfy the chain.
Show a hint
  • Work on all three parts at each step, the same way 8.3 solved a chain, and keep track of which end carries the strict symbol.
  • Subtracting 33 from all three parts gives −8<2x≤14−8<2x≤14. Divide all three by the positive 22, then count the integers between the two ends, remembering that the end with the strict symbol is drawn open and is left out.
Show the full solution
Subtracting 33 from all three parts gives −8<2x≤14−8<2x≤14, and dividing all three by the positive 22 gives −4<x≤7−4<x≤7. The integers on the segment run from −3−3 to 77, and 7−(−3)+1=117−(−3)+1=11​. The end at −4−4 is drawn open, so −4−4 is left out, while the end at 77 is drawn filled, so 77 is counted.
Problem
The point (9,7)(9,7) lies on the line y=3x−20y=3x−20. Enter yes if (9,7)(9,7) is a solution of y<3x−20y<3x−20, and no if it is not.
Show a hint
  • Substitute the point, putting 99 in for xx and 77 in for yy, then check whether the resulting statement is true.
  • The point is on the line, so the two sides come out equal. The question is whether << is true when the two sides are equal.
Show the full solution
Substituting gives 7<3(9)−207<3(9)−20, which is 7<77<7, false, so the answer is nono​. A strict inequality is false wherever the two sides are equal, so no point of the line y=3x−20y=3x−20 is a solution, just as an open circle on a number line means the endpoint is not included.
Key idea
The graph of an inequality is the set of points that satisfy it. That is 7.2's definition of a graph with the equals sign replaced. A number is on the graph of x≤3x≤3 when substituting it makes the statement true, and a point (x,y)(x,y) is on the graph of y>4x−1y>4x−1 when substituting both coordinates makes it true. The one difference from an equation is how many points make it true. A linear equation in two letters is true only at the points of one line, so its graph is thin, while a linear inequality is true across whole areas, so its graph is a region.

With one letter the boundary is a single point. With two letters it is the set of points where the two sides come out equal, the line y=mx+by=mx+b that chapter 7 drew. Every other point of the plane sits on one side of it or the other, and two things are undecided, which side is the graph and whether the line belongs to it.

Problem
The line y=5x−14y=5x−14 splits the plane into two sides, and y>5x−14y>5x−14 is true at every point of one side and false at every point of the other. The origin is not on that line, so substituting (0,0)(0,0) settles which side is which. Enter the word above or below for the side that holds the solutions.
Show a hint
  • Substituting the origin puts 00 in for both letters, which leaves only the constant term on the right.
  • A true test means the origin is one of the solutions, so the side you want is the side the origin sits on. Put x=0x=0 into 5x−145x−14 for the line's height there, then compare it with the origin's height of 00.
Show the full solution
Substituting (0,0)(0,0) gives 0>−140>−14, which is true, so the origin is one of the solutions. At x=0x=0 the line is at y=−14y=−14 while the origin is at y=0y=0, so the origin's side is the one aboveabove​. Testing one point settles the whole side, since the inequality is true at every point of one side and false at every point of the other.
Problem
The point (12,16)(12,16) lies on the line y=53x−4y=35​x−4, which is the boundary of y≥53x−4y≥35​x−4. A boundary is drawn dashed when its own points are not solutions and solid when they are. Decide whether (12,16)(12,16) is a solution, then enter the word, dashed or solid.
Show a hint
  • The word depends on one yes or no question, whether the points of the boundary line are solutions. Substitute (12,16)(12,16), a point of that line, and see whether the inequality holds.
  • The right side at x=12x=12 is 53(12)−435​(12)−4, which is 20−420−4. Compare that with the point's yy-coordinate of 1616.
Show the full solution
The right side at x=12x=12 is 53(12)−4=1635​(12)−4=16, the point's own yy-coordinate, and 16≥1616≥16 is true, so (12,16)(12,16) is a solution and the boundary is drawn solidsolid​. Every point of the line makes the two sides equal, so one check settles all of them. Under >> and << equality is not allowed and the boundary is dashed, the number line's open and filled circles one dimension up.
Key idea
The graph of y>mx+by>mx+b is the half-plane above the line y=mx+by=mx+b. Take any point (x0,y0)(x0​,y0​) of that line, so y0=mx0+by0​=mx0​+b, and move straight up. The first coordinate is still x0x0​, so the right side is still mx0+bmx0​+b, while the second coordinate is larger, so the statement is true there, and straight down it is false. Every point of the plane is above the line, below it, or on it, so every solution is above and none is below. The boundary is drawn dashed for a strict symbol and solid for ≥≥ or ≤≤, which is the open and filled circle one dimension up.

The statement is true at every point of one side of the boundary and false at every point of the other, so substituting one point that is off the boundary settles the shaded side. The origin is the cheapest test, since substituting it puts zero in for both letters, and it works whenever the boundary line does not pass through it.

Problem
The boundary of y>32xy>23​x is a line through the origin, so (0,0)(0,0) is not available as a test point. Enter the smallest integer yy for which (6,y)(6,y) is a solution.
Show a hint
  • Put x=6x=6 into the inequality. The right side becomes a single number, so what is left is an inequality in yy alone.
  • That number is 32(6)23​(6), and the symbol is strict, so the boundary value itself is not a solution. The answer is the first integer above it.
Show the full solution
At x=6x=6 the inequality reads y>32(6)y>23​(6), which is y>9y>9, so the smallest integer is 1010​. The origin lies on the boundary and settles nothing, while (6,10)(6,10) lies off it and satisfies the inequality, so the shaded side is the one above the line.
Fun fact
Leonid Kantorovich was asked in the late 1930s to get the most out of a plywood factory's machines. He turned it into a question about the region of plans allowed by a list of inequalities, and linear programming began there.
Problem
The inequality 3x−4y>203x−4y>20 is not solved for yy. Enter the largest integer yy for which the point (8,y)(8,y) satisfies this inequality.
Show a hint
  • Substituting x=8x=8 leaves an inequality in yy alone. Check the sign of the coefficient of yy before dividing, since 8.1's rule about dividing by a negative applies.
  • That inequality is 24−4y>2024−4y>20, so −4y>−4−4y>−4. Dividing both sides by −4−4 reverses the direction.
Show the full solution
Substituting x=8x=8 gives 24−4y>2024−4y>20, so −4y>−4−4y>−4, and dividing by −4−4 reverses the direction to y<1y<1. The largest integer below 11 is 00​. Checking, 3(8)−4(0)=24>203(8)−4(0)=24>20, while 3(8)−4(1)=203(8)−4(1)=20 is not above 2020. Keeping >> through that division would give y>1y>1, which has no largest integer at all.
Key idea
An inequality written ax+by≤cax+by≤c can be graphed by either of two routes. One is to solve for yy first, where 8.1's rule applies to the final division, so a negative bb reverses the direction. Solving 3x−4y>203x−4y>20 that way gives y<3x−204y<43x−20​, so the solutions are below the boundary even though the symbol is >>. The other route leaves the form alone. Draw ax+by=cax+by=c from its intercepts the 7.5 way and test one point off it, shading its side if the test is true and the other side if it is false. Nothing is divided, so no direction reverses.

Several inequalities can hold at once, and a point is a solution only when it satisfies them all. Each has its own half-plane, and some have only one letter. The inequality x≥kx≥k says nothing about yy, so its graph is every point on or right of the vertical line x=kx=k, and y<ky<k graphs as everything below the horizontal line y=ky=k.

Problem
In the plane the graph of x≥−6x≥−6 is a half-plane. Enter how many of the points (−6,25)(−6,25), (−132,0)(−213​,0), (3,−41)(3,−41), (−7,−7)(−7,−7) and (−5,12)(−5,12) satisfy x≥−6x≥−6.
Show a hint
  • The inequality is a condition on xx alone, so compare each first coordinate with −6−6 and ignore the second one entirely.
  • Two of the five are close calls. One turns on whether ≥≥ is true when the two sides are equal, and the other on how −132−213​ compares with −6−6.
Show the full solution
Only the first coordinate matters. −6≥−6−6≥−6 is true, −132≥−6−213​≥−6 is false, 3≥−63≥−6 is true, −7≥−6−7≥−6 is false, and −5≥−6−5≥−6 is true, so the count is 33​. The graph is the vertical line x=−6x=−6 drawn solid together with everything to its right, and the second coordinate is free because yy never appears in it.
Problem
A point is on the graph of two inequalities at once exactly when both substitutions come out true. Enter how many of (3,4)(3,4), (4,7)(4,7), (5,4)(5,4), (6,5)(6,5), (2,1)(2,1) and (7,6)(7,6) satisfy both y<2x−1y<2x−1 and x+y≥7x+y≥7.
Show a hint
  • Each inequality has its own half-plane, so every point needs two substitutions, and one false result is enough to leave it out.
  • Two of the points sit on a boundary. (4,7)(4,7) makes the first read 7<77<7 and (3,4)(3,4) makes the second read 7≥77≥7, and only one of those two symbols is true when the sides are equal.
Show the full solution
(3,4)(3,4), (5,4)(5,4), (6,5)(6,5) and (7,6)(7,6) satisfy both, so the count is 44​. (4,7)(4,7) gives 7<77<7, false, and (2,1)(2,1) gives 3≥73≥7, false. Of the two points on a boundary, (3,4)(3,4) is included and (4,7)(4,7) is not, since x+y=7x+y=7 is drawn solid under ≥≥ while y=2x−1y=2x−1 is drawn dashed under <<.
Key idea
The graph of several inequalities at once is the overlap of their half-planes. A point belongs when every substitution comes out true, so one false substitution is enough to leave it out. A corner of that region is a point where two of the boundary lines cross, and its coordinates come from solving those two boundary equations as a system, which is chapter 5's work and 7.6's picture. A crossing counts as a corner only when it also satisfies the inequalities that were not used to find it, and a crossing on a dashed boundary is at the edge of the region without being part of it.

The work is two moves per inequality. Draw the boundary, dashed for a strict symbol and solid otherwise, then test one point off it to decide which side is shaded. A region closed on every side contains finitely many points with integer coordinates, and those are counted one column at a time, fixing xx and reading which yy are allowed.

Problem
The points that satisfy all three of x≥1x≥1, y≥2y≥2 and 3x+2y≤203x+2y≤20 form a triangular region, and the edges are part of the region. Enter how many points with integer coordinates lie in that region.
Show a hint
  • Count one vertical line at a time. Since y≥2y≥2, every point in the region has 3x≤20−4=163x≤20−4=16, so xx is at most 55.
  • Set x=1x=1 in the third inequality to get 2y≤172y≤17, so yy is an integer from 22 to 88. Do the same at each xx and add the counts.
Show the full solution
At x=1x=1 the third inequality becomes 2y≤172y≤17, so yy is an integer from 22 to 88 and that column has 77 points, and the same count at x=2,3,4,5x=2,3,4,5 is 66, 44, 33 and 11, with nothing left at x=6x=6, so the total is 7+6+4+3+1=217+6+4+3+1=21​. At x=1x=1, x=3x=3 and x=5x=5 the bound on yy is not a whole number, so the largest integer yy is below it.
Problem
The points that satisfy 3x+4y≤263x+4y≤26, x−2y≥−3x−2y≥−3 and y≥0y≥0 all at once form a triangular region. Two of its corners sit on the xx-axis, and the third is where the boundary lines of the first two inequalities cross. Enter the yy-coordinate of that third corner.
Show a hint
  • The two boundary lines are 3x+4y=263x+4y=26 and x−2y=−3x−2y=−3, and the corner is the one point on both of them, so finding it is a chapter 5 system.
  • The second equation gives x=2y−3x=2y−3. Substituting that into the first leaves an equation in yy alone.
Show the full solution
The boundaries are 3x+4y=263x+4y=26 and x−2y=−3x−2y=−3. The second gives x=2y−3x=2y−3, and substituting gives 3(2y−3)+4y=263(2y−3)+4y=26, so 10y−9=2610y−9=26 and y=72y=27​​. The corner is (4,72)(4,27​), and y≥0y≥0 holds there, so it really is a corner of the region.

Every region in this lesson was drawn and then read, for a count of the points inside it or for one corner. Nothing here asked which point of a region is the best one. Lesson 8.5, Optimization, asks exactly that, and the corners found here are the points to check.

Practice these ideas

Practice
The solutions of x−14>9x−14>9 fill a ray on the number line, and the ray does not include the number it starts at. Enter that number.
Show the solution
Adding 1414 to both sides leaves the direction alone and gives x>23x>23​. At x=23x=23 the statement reads 9>99>9, which is false, so the ray starts at 2323 without including it.
Practice
Solve 5x+7≤−135x+7≤−13. The solutions form a ray on the number line with a single circle at its endpoint. Enter one word, open or filled, for that circle.
Show the solution
Subtracting 77 gives 5x≤−205x≤−20, and dividing both sides by the positive 55 leaves the direction alone, so x≤−4x≤−4. At x=−4x=−4 the left side is exactly −13−13, and ≤≤ allows equality, so the circle is filledfilled​. Everything to the left of −4−4 is shaded, and −4−4 is included in the solution set.
Practice
The solutions of −7<3x+2≤14−7<3x+2≤14 form a segment with one end included and the other excluded. Enter the number at the excluded end.
Show the solution
Subtracting 22 gives −9<3x≤12−9<3x≤12, and dividing by 33 gives −3<x≤4−3<x≤4, so the excluded end is −3−3​. The strict symbol is at the lower end, so the open circle is at −3−3 and the filled one is at 44.
Practice
Enter yes if (6,−1)(6,−1) satisfies y>13x−5y>31​x−5, and no if it does not.
Show the solution
The right side is 13(6)−5=−331​(6)−5=−3, and −1>−3−1>−3 is true, so the answer is yesyes​. On the number line −1−1 sits to the right of −3−3, which is what makes it the larger of the two.
Practice
The graph of y<7x+2y<7x+2 is a half-plane. Enter one word, dashed or solid, for how its boundary line is drawn.
Show the solution
At a point of y=7x+2y=7x+2 the two sides are equal, and << is strict, so those points are not solutions and the line is drawn dasheddashed​. A dashed boundary means its points are excluded, the same convention as an open circle on a number line.
Practice
Test the origin in y≤−4x+9y≤−4x+9 to settle which side of the boundary line y=−4x+9y=−4x+9 holds the solutions. Enter the word above or below.
Show the solution
Substituting (0,0)(0,0) gives 0≤90≤9, which is true, so the origin is a solution. At x=0x=0 the origin is at y=0y=0 while the line is at y=9y=9, so the solutions lie belowbelow​. Checking the other side, (0,20)(0,20) gives 20≤920≤9, which is false.
Practice
The graph of y<6y<6 in the plane is a half-plane. Enter how many of the seven points (11,6)(11,6), (−2,5)(−2,5), (0,−30)(0,−30), (4,132)(4,213​), (7,−1)(7,−1), (−9,0)(−9,0) and (15,5)(15,5) satisfy y<6y<6.
Show the solution
Only the second coordinate matters, and the points with second coordinate below 66 are (−2,5)(−2,5), (0,−30)(0,−30), (7,−1)(7,−1), (−9,0)(−9,0) and (15,5)(15,5), so the count is 55​. The other two fail because 132=6.5213​=6.5 is more than 66, and (11,6)(11,6) is on the boundary line, where the strict 6<66<6 is false.
Practice
In the plane the graph of 3x+4<433x+4<43 is a half-plane whose boundary is a vertical line. Enter the xx-coordinate that every point of that boundary has.
Show the solution
Subtracting 44 gives 3x<393x<39, and dividing by the positive 33 gives x<13x<13​. The shaded region is everything to the left of the line x=13x=13, and that line is drawn dashed, since the bound is strict.
Practice
The graph of 6x+y≥56x+y≥5 is a half-plane, and its boundary line is part of it. Enter the smallest integer yy for which (−2,y)(−2,y) lies in that half-plane.
Show the solution
Substituting x=−2x=−2 gives −12+y≥5−12+y≥5, so y≥17y≥17 and the smallest integer available is 1717​. The inequality is not strict, so 1717 itself counts. Checking, 6(−2)+17=56(−2)+17=5, and 5≥55≥5 is true.
Practice
The graph of 2x+3y≤312x+3y≤31 is a half-plane. Enter the largest integer yy for which the point (5,y)(5,y) lies in it.
Show the solution
Substituting gives 10+3y≤3110+3y≤31, so 3y≤213y≤21 and y≤7y≤7​. Checking, 2(5)+3(7)=312(5)+3(7)=31, and 31≤3131≤31 is true, so 77 is allowed.
Practice
Enter the smallest integer yy for which the point (3,y)(3,y) satisfies 4x−5y≤−284x−5y≤−28.
Show the solution
Substituting x=3x=3 gives 12−5y≤−2812−5y≤−28, so −5y≤−40−5y≤−40, and dividing by −5−5 reverses the direction to y≥8y≥8​. At y=8y=8 the left side is 12−40=−2812−40=−28, and a ≤≤ statement is true when the two sides are equal, so 88 itself works, while y=7y=7 gives −23−23, which is greater than −28−28.
Practice
The origin lies on the boundary line of y>54xy>45​x, so a test point has to come from somewhere off that line. Enter the smallest integer yy for which (20,y)(20,y) is a solution.
Show the solution
At x=20x=20 the inequality reads y>25y>25, so the smallest integer is 2626​. The point (20,26)(20,26) is then a usable test point, and it sits above the line, so the graph is the region above.
Practice
Enter how many of the six points (0,0)(0,0), (1,6)(1,6), (5,1)(5,1), (3,5)(3,5), (2,1)(2,1) and (4,0)(4,0) satisfy both y≤x+2y≤x+2 and x+y>4x+y>4.
Show the solution
(5,1)(5,1) gives 1≤71≤7 and 6>46>4, and (3,5)(3,5) gives 5≤55≤5 and 8>48>4, so both pass. (1,6)(1,6) fails the first, and (0,0)(0,0), (2,1)(2,1) and (4,0)(4,0) fail the second, so the count is 22​. The two boundary cases come out differently because ≤≤ includes its boundary line, drawn solid, while >> excludes its own, drawn dashed.
Practice
The boundary lines of x+y≤20x+y≤20 and x−y≥4x−y≥4 cross at one point. Enter the xx-coordinate of that point.
Show the solution
Adding x+y=20x+y=20 and x−y=4x−y=4 gives 2x=242x=24, so x=12x=12​. The crossing is (12,8)(12,8), and both inequalities hold there with equality, so it is a corner of the region they share.
Practice
Enter how many points with integer coordinates satisfy all three of x≥0x≥0, y≥0y≥0 and 2x+y≤62x+y≤6.
Show the solution
At x=0x=0 the allowed yy run from 00 to 66, which is 77 points, then 55 at x=1x=1, 33 at x=2x=2 and 11 at x=3x=3, so the count is 7+5+3+1=167+5+3+1=16​. All three inequalities are non-strict, so the points on all three edges are counted.
Practice
The inequality 6x−3y<126x−3y<12 is graphed in the plane. Enter the word, above or below, for the side of its boundary line where the solutions lie.
Show the solution
Subtracting 6x6x gives −3y<12−6x−3y<12−6x, and dividing by −3−3 reverses the direction to y>2x−4y>2x−4, so the solutions lie aboveabove​. Testing the origin gives the true statement 0<120<12, and the origin sits above y=2x−4y=2x−4, which crosses the yy-axis at −4−4.
Practice
The boundary lines of 3x−2y≥−43x−2y≥−4 and x+2y≤16x+2y≤16 cross at a corner of the region where both hold. Enter the yy-coordinate of that corner.
Show the solution
Adding 3x−2y=−43x−2y=−4 and x+2y=16x+2y=16 gives 4x=124x=12, so x=3x=3, and 3+2y=163+2y=16 gives y=132y=213​​. Both ≥≥ and ≤≤ allow equality, so their boundary lines are solid and the corner (3,132)(3,213​) is itself in the region.
